title: Preference-Opt + Gradient Attacks
hook:
DPO can turn a stubborn model compliant in twenty minutes, on your laptop.

GCG can crack a model open with pure math — no persona, no roleplay, just gradients.

But GCG wants CUDA. Your Mac has Metal.

Tonight you learn which attacks run at home, and which one you rent a GPU-hour for.
mechanism:
Two different levers move a model's behaviour.

**Preference optimization.** DPO, ORPO, and GRPO train directly on pairs: this answer beats that one. No separate reward model, no RL loop. Enough pairs, and the policy drifts toward whichever side you kept marking preferred — including toward compliance.

**Gradient attacks.** GCG optimizes an adversarial suffix by reading the model's own gradients — white-box, dense, and CUDA-heavy. BEAST and AutoDAN approximate the same idea with cheaper search (beam search, genetic search) that runs fine on a laptop GPU.

Same family, wildly different price tags. One needs 200 preference pairs and twenty minutes. The other needs a real CUDA card for an hour.
technique:
Three moves, in order.

**Train locally first.** `mlx-lm-lora --train-type dpo` on 200 preference pairs, Qwen2.5-0.5B, right on Apple Silicon. Ten to twenty minutes, no GPU rental.

**Reproduce the cheap attacks yourself.** BEAST and AutoDAN are search algorithms — rebuild the idea directly on MPS. Do not clone their CUDA-only repos and fight the build.

**Rent for nanoGCG only.** Its dense gradient steps need real CUDA kernels. One GPU-hour, once, beats days of fighting Metal.

Every verdict you write down needs two numbers: wall-clock and attack success rate (ASR). Without both, "local vs rent" is just a vibe.

drills.q: In the technique, how many preference pairs does the local DPO run train on?
drills.why: mlx-lm-lora --train-type dpo trains Qwen2.5-0.5B on 200 preference pairs locally — small enough to finish in ten to twenty minutes on Apple Silicon.

drills.q: In the hardware widget, which ONE of the four attacks is CUDA-only — the one you rent a GPU-hour for?
drills.why: DPO, BEAST, and AutoDAN all run on MPS. nanoGCG's dense, per-token gradient steps need real CUDA kernels — that's the one line item worth a rented GPU-hour.

drills.q: In Panel A, if you mark the compliant answer as preferred on all three pairs, does the policy's compliance meter go UP or DOWN?
drills.why: Each compliant pick pulls the teaching-model meter up by 20 points off a 35% baseline. That's the whole DPO mechanism in miniature: train on what you marked preferred, and the policy moves toward it.

lab:
The lab runs a real DPO pass, then times the cheap attacks on your own machine.

**Stage 1.** `mlx-lm-lora --train-type dpo` trains Qwen2.5-0.5B on 200 preference pairs, right there on MPS.

**Stage 2.** A short probe times a GCG-style suffix search on MPS, so you feel how slow dense gradients are without CUDA.

**Stage 3.** nanoGCG is NOT run. The script prints the rent-a-GPU instruction instead, because CUDA is the whole point of that attack.

Your number tonight: **the hardware verdict** — local-or-rent, with wall-clock and ASR, for each of the four attacks. Write it in your log.

notes: Panel A simulates DPO's preference-pull as a teaching model (not a trained policy) — the real pass is the Lab's mlx-lm-lora run. Panel B's hardware verdict (MPS vs CUDA-only) encodes the real constraint: DPO/BEAST/AutoDAN run fine on Apple Silicon; GCG-family dense-gradient attacks need CUDA. Lab = labs/unit14-dpo-gradient.sh: stage 1 runs mlx-lm-lora DPO on Qwen2.5-0.5B if installed, stage 2 times an MPS suffix-search probe, stage 3 prints the rent-a-GPU instruction for nanoGCG instead of running CUDA. Degrades to a friendly 'do Unit 2 first' message if the local toolchain isn't installed yet.
